question.text: Who counts as a pedestrian under Tennessee law?

answer.text: Under Tennessee law, anyone on foot or using a motorized or non-motorized wheelchair counts as a pedestrian.

teaching.text: Asked "Under Tennessee law, does a person using a motorized wheelchair count as a pedestrian?" a tempting wrong answer is "No, only people on foot", but wheelchair users count too. Remember: Wheelchairs count too.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under Tennessee law, anyone on foot or using a motorized or non-motorized wheelchair counts as a pedestrian.

question.text: Where do pedestrians generally have the right-of-way?

answer.text: Pedestrians generally have the right-of-way at all intersections, and every intersection has a crosswalk even when no lines are painted.

teaching.text: Asked "An intersection has no painted crosswalk lines. Is there a crosswalk?" a tempting wrong answer is "No, only painted ones count", but every intersection has one. Remember: Every intersection has a crosswalk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians generally have the right-of-way at all intersections, and every intersection has a crosswalk even when no lines are painted.

question.text: What care must drivers always use around pedestrians?

answer.text: Whatever the right-of-way rules say, the law requires drivers to use great care and extreme caution to avoid hitting pedestrians.

teaching.text: Asked "Whatever the right-of-way rules say, what does the law require of drivers around pedestrians?" a tempting wrong answer is "Nothing if the pedestrian is wrong", but great care is always required. Remember: Extreme caution always.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Whatever the right-of-way rules say, the law requires drivers to use great care and extreme caution to avoid hitting pedestrians.

question.text: Why not stop over the crosswalk at a red light?

answer.text: Do not stop with any part of your vehicle over the crosswalk at a red light or while waiting to turn, because it forces pedestrians around your car.

teaching.text: Asked "You stop at a red light. Where should the front of your car be?" a tempting wrong answer is "Halfway into the crosswalk", but keep off the crosswalk. Remember: Keep crosswalks clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not stop with any part of your vehicle over the crosswalk at a red light or while waiting to turn, because it forces pedestrians around your car.

question.text: Who are the most frequent victims of car-pedestrian crashes?

answer.text: Young, elderly, disabled and intoxicated pedestrians are the most frequent victims of car-pedestrian crashes, so watch for them especially.

teaching.text: Asked "Which pedestrians are the most frequent victims of car-pedestrian crashes?" a tempting wrong answer is "Joggers only", but young, elderly, disabled and intoxicated. Remember: Watch vulnerable walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Young, elderly, disabled and intoxicated pedestrians are the most frequent victims of car-pedestrian crashes, so watch for them especially.

question.text: When must you yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk?

answer.text: Yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk who is on your half of the road, or so close to it from the other half as to be in danger.

teaching.text: The school zone crosswalks rule requires stopping for crossing pedestrians in a flashing school zone, while the your half of the road rule requires yielding to a pedestrian on your half of the road. Remember: Your half or close.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk who is on your half of the road, or so close to it from the other half as to be in danger.

question.text: Where should you watch for pedestrians when turning right?

answer.text: Watch for pedestrians on your right, especially when you are making a right turn.

teaching.text: Asked "When should you especially watch for pedestrians on your right?" a tempting wrong answer is "When backing", but when making a right turn. Remember: Look right for walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for pedestrians on your right, especially when you are making a right turn.

question.text: Which pedestrians are least predictable?

answer.text: Children are the least predictable and hardest-to-see pedestrians, so take extra care near school zones, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and snack vendors.

teaching.text: Asked "Which pedestrians are the least predictable and hardest to see?" a tempting wrong answer is "Adults with briefcases", but children. Remember: Children are unpredictable.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children are the least predictable and hardest-to-see pedestrians, so take extra care near school zones, bus stops, playgrounds, parks and snack vendors.

question.text: Whom must you yield to when crossing a sidewalk at a driveway?

answer.text: Yield to people on the sidewalk when you enter or leave a driveway, alley, parking lot or garage across it, and never honk or rev your engine to rush a pedestrian.

teaching.text: Asked "You are leaving a parking garage across a sidewalk. What must you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Honk to clear them", but never honk to rush them. Remember: Sidewalk walkers first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yield to people on the sidewalk when you enter or leave a driveway, alley, parking lot or garage across it, and never honk or rev your engine to rush a pedestrian.

question.text: What must you do for a crossing pedestrian in a flashing school zone?

answer.text: In a marked school zone with its warning flashers on, you must stop for a pedestrian crossing in a marked crosswalk or at an intersection without one, and stay stopped until the pedestrian has crossed your roadway.

teaching.text: The school zone crosswalks rule requires stopping for crossing pedestrians in a flashing school zone, while the your half of the road rule requires yielding to a pedestrian on your half of the road. Remember: Stop until they cross.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a marked school zone with its warning flashers on, you must stop for a pedestrian crossing in a marked crosswalk or at an intersection without one, and stay stopped until the pedestrian has crossed your roadway.

question.text: Whom must you always yield to with a cane or guide dog?

answer.text: Always yield to a blind pedestrian carrying a white or metallic cane with a red tip or using a guide dog.

teaching.text: The blind pedestrians rule requires yielding to blind pedestrians with a cane or guide dog, while the school zone crosswalks rule requires stopping in a flashing school zone. Remember: Yield to blind walkers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always yield to a blind pedestrian carrying a white or metallic cane with a red tip or using a guide dog.

question.text: Where must pedestrians walk when sidewalks exist?

answer.text: Where sidewalks exist, pedestrians must use them, and walking in the road there is illegal.

teaching.text: The use the sidewalk rule requires pedestrians to use sidewalks where they exist, while the walk facing traffic rule says to walk facing traffic where there is none. Remember: Use the sidewalk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where sidewalks exist, pedestrians must use them, and walking in the road there is illegal.

question.text: Where should you walk where there is no sidewalk?

answer.text: Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the left side of the road facing oncoming traffic, in single file when walking with others.

teaching.text: The use the sidewalk rule requires pedestrians to use sidewalks where they exist, while the walk facing traffic rule says to walk facing traffic where there is none. Remember: Left side, facing traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where there is no sidewalk, walk on the left side of the road facing oncoming traffic, in single file when walking with others.

question.text: Why avoid headphones when walking beside busy roads?

answer.text: Walking or jogging beside busy roads with headphones on can keep you from hearing traffic warnings.

teaching.text: Asked "Why avoid headphones while jogging beside busy roads?" a tempting wrong answer is "They are too heavy", but you may miss traffic warnings. Remember: Hear the traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Walking or jogging beside busy roads with headphones on can keep you from hearing traffic warnings.

question.text: How should a pedestrian look before crossing?

answer.text: Before crossing, stop at the curb or road edge and look left, right and left again, then check over your shoulder for turning vehicles.

teaching.text: Asked "Before crossing, how should a pedestrian look?" a tempting wrong answer is "Only straight ahead", but left, right, left, then shoulder. Remember: Left, right, left, shoulder.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before crossing, stop at the curb or road edge and look left, right and left again, then check over your shoulder for turning vehicles.

question.text: Why step back at corners when trucks turn?

answer.text: Trucks and buses make wide right turns that can run up onto the corner of the sidewalk, so pedestrians on corners should step back.

teaching.text: Asked "A bus is making a right turn at your corner. What should you do as a pedestrian?" a tempting wrong answer is "Step into the street", but step back. Remember: Wide turns hit corners.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks and buses make wide right turns that can run up onto the corner of the sidewalk, so pedestrians on corners should step back.

question.text: Why never walk behind a backing truck?

answer.text: Never walk behind a truck that is backing up, because its driver cannot see directly behind it.

teaching.text: Asked "A truck is backing up. Why should you never walk behind it?" a tempting wrong answer is "It is fine if it beeps", but the driver cannot see behind. Remember: Backing drivers cannot see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never walk behind a truck that is backing up, because its driver cannot see directly behind it.

question.text: How can pedestrians be seen at night?

answer.text: At night, pedestrians should wear bright or reflective clothing, and carrying a flashlight is the safest way to be seen.

teaching.text: Asked "What is the safest way for a pedestrian to be seen at night?" a tempting wrong answer is "Wearing dark clothes", but carry a flashlight. Remember: Bright clothes, flashlight.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, pedestrians should wear bright or reflective clothing, and carrying a flashlight is the safest way to be seen.

question.text: Does a WALK signal mean it is safe to cross?

answer.text: A WALK signal or a green light means it is your turn to cross, not that it is safe; look first and cross only if it is safe.

teaching.text: Asked "What does a WALK signal mean?" a tempting wrong answer is "It is always safe", but it is your turn, not a guarantee. Remember: Your turn, not safe.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A WALK signal or a green light means it is your turn to cross, not that it is safe; look first and cross only if it is safe.

question.text: What should you do if DON'T WALK flashes mid-street?

answer.text: If the DON'T WALK signal starts flashing while you are mid-street, keep walking, because you will have time to finish crossing.

teaching.text: Asked "The DON'T WALK signal starts flashing while you are mid-street. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Turn back at once", but keep walking. Remember: Keep walking across.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the DON'T WALK signal starts flashing while you are mid-street, keep walking, because you will have time to finish crossing.

question.text: When may pedestrians not cross?

answer.text: Pedestrians may not cross on a red or yellow light, or on a mixed red and green turn light, unless facing a WALK signal.

teaching.text: Asked "May pedestrians cross on a yellow light without a WALK signal?" a tempting wrong answer is "Yes, quickly", but not without a WALK signal. Remember: Red or yellow, wait.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians may not cross on a red or yellow light, or on a mixed red and green turn light, unless facing a WALK signal.

question.text: Why not step out in front of a close vehicle?

answer.text: Pedestrians must not step off the curb into the path of a vehicle so close that it is an immediate hazard, because vehicles cannot stop at once.

teaching.text: Asked "Why must pedestrians not step into the path of a close vehicle?" a tempting wrong answer is "Drivers must always stop", but vehicles cannot stop at once. Remember: Cars cannot stop instantly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pedestrians must not step off the curb into the path of a vehicle so close that it is an immediate hazard, because vehicles cannot stop at once.

question.text: What are the most common car-bicycle crashes?

answer.text: The most common car-bicycle crashes happen when a driver turns left in front of an oncoming bicycle or turns right across a bicycle's path.

teaching.text: The common bicycle crashes rule names left and right turns as the common bicycle crashes, and the turning near bicyclists rule says to let the rider pass first. Remember: Turns across bicycles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The most common car-bicycle crashes happen when a driver turns left in front of an oncoming bicycle or turns right across a bicycle's path.

question.text: What should you do when turning near a bicyclist?

answer.text: When turning left with a bicyclist coming from the opposite direction, wait for the rider to pass; when turning right with a bicyclist approaching on your right, let the rider through first.

teaching.text: The common bicycle crashes rule names left and right turns as the common bicycle crashes, and the turning near bicyclists rule says to let the rider pass first. Remember: Let the rider pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When turning left with a bicyclist coming from the opposite direction, wait for the rider to pass; when turning right with a bicyclist approaching on your right, let the rider through first.

question.text: What rights do bicyclists have, and where are they banned?

answer.text: On most roads bicyclists have the same rights and duties as other road users, but they are banned from limited-access highways, expressways and certain marked roads.

teaching.text: Asked "Where are bicyclists banned in Tennessee?" a tempting wrong answer is "All city streets", but they have rights on most roads. Remember: Same rights, not expressways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On most roads bicyclists have the same rights and duties as other road users, but they are banned from limited-access highways, expressways and certain marked roads.

question.text: Where must bicyclists ride?

answer.text: Bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road in the same direction as traffic, as far right as practical while avoiding hazards.

teaching.text: Asked "Where must bicyclists ride?" a tempting wrong answer is "On the left facing traffic", but on the right with traffic. Remember: Right side, with traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists must ride on the right side of the road in the same direction as traffic, as far right as practical while avoiding hazards.

question.text: Why may a bicyclist ride toward the center of the lane?

answer.text: When a bicyclist rides away from parked cars toward the center of the lane, the rider is riding properly to avoid opening doors.

teaching.text: The riding away from doors rule says riding toward the lane's center away from parked cars is proper, and the taking the full lane rule lists when a bicyclist may take the full lane. Remember: Away from opening doors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a bicyclist rides away from parked cars toward the center of the lane, the rider is riding properly to avoid opening doors.

question.text: How much room must you give when passing a bicycle?

answer.text: Tennessee law requires you to pass a bicycle going your way slowly and with at least three feet of clearance, keeping that space until you are safely past.

teaching.text: The three feet to pass rule requires at least three feet when passing a bicycle, while the do not squeeze past rule forbids passing between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic. Remember: Three feet to pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tennessee law requires you to pass a bicycle going your way slowly and with at least three feet of clearance, keeping that space until you are safely past.

question.text: May you pass between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic?

answer.text: Never pass between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic on a two-lane road; slow down and wait until it is safe.

teaching.text: The three feet to pass rule requires at least three feet when passing a bicycle, while the do not squeeze past rule forbids passing between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic. Remember: Never squeeze past.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never pass between a bicyclist and oncoming traffic on a two-lane road; slow down and wait until it is safe.

question.text: How should you share a turn lane with a bicyclist?

answer.text: If you share a left turn lane with a bicyclist, stay behind the rider until the turn is complete, and before a right turn merge with bicycle traffic rather than cutting across it.

teaching.text: Asked "You share a left turn lane with a bicyclist. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Pass in the lane", but stay behind the rider. Remember: Stay behind the rider.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you share a left turn lane with a bicyclist, stay behind the rider until the turn is complete, and before a right turn merge with bicycle traffic rather than cutting across it.

question.text: Where should you never pass a bicycle?

answer.text: Never pass a bicycle where the street is too narrow or the pass would push the rider close to parked cars.

teaching.text: Asked "Where should you never pass a bicycle?" a tempting wrong answer is "On wide roads", but never where it is too narrow. Remember: No pass on narrow streets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never pass a bicycle where the street is too narrow or the pass would push the rider close to parked cars.

question.text: How should you use the horn before passing a bicyclist?

answer.text: Before passing a bicycle on a narrow road when the rider may not know you are there, tap the horn gently and briefly instead of blasting it.

teaching.text: Asked "Before passing a bicyclist on a narrow road who may not know you are there, what may you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Blast the horn", but tap gently. Remember: Tap, never blast.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before passing a bicycle on a narrow road when the rider may not know you are there, tap the horn gently and briefly instead of blasting it.

question.text: May drivers use a bicycle-only lane to turn or park?

answer.text: A marked and signed bicycle-only lane must never be used by drivers for turning, passing or parking.

teaching.text: Asked "May a driver use a marked bicycle-only lane to park?" a tempting wrong answer is "Yes, briefly", but never. Remember: Bike lanes stay clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A marked and signed bicycle-only lane must never be used by drivers for turning, passing or parking.

question.text: Which beams should you use for an oncoming bicyclist at night?

answer.text: At night, do not use your high beams when you see an oncoming bicyclist.

teaching.text: Asked "At night you see an oncoming bicyclist. Which beams should you use?" a tempting wrong answer is "High beams to see them", but do not use high beams. Remember: Dim for bicycles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night, do not use your high beams when you see an oncoming bicyclist.

question.text: What are the turn hand signals?

answer.text: Hand signals: a left turn is the left arm straight out, and a right turn is the left arm bent up at the elbow or the right arm straight out.

teaching.text: The turn hand signals rule covers the left and right turn signals, while the stop hand signal rule covers the arm bent downward to stop or slow. Remember: Straight left, bent up right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals: a left turn is the left arm straight out, and a right turn is the left arm bent up at the elbow or the right arm straight out.

question.text: What is the stop or slow hand signal?

answer.text: The hand signal for stopping or slowing is an arm held out and bent downward at the elbow, with the palm facing back.

teaching.text: The turn hand signals rule covers the left and right turn signals, while the stop hand signal rule covers the arm bent downward to stop or slow. Remember: Arm bent downward.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The hand signal for stopping or slowing is an arm held out and bent downward at the elbow, with the palm facing back.

question.text: When may a bicyclist take the full lane?

answer.text: A bicyclist may take the full lane when passing another vehicle, when the road has hazards such as potholes, debris or parked cars, or when the lane is too narrow to share.

teaching.text: The riding away from doors rule says riding toward the lane's center away from parked cars is proper, and the taking the full lane rule lists when a bicyclist may take the full lane. Remember: Hazards or narrow lanes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A bicyclist may take the full lane when passing another vehicle, when the road has hazards such as potholes, debris or parked cars, or when the lane is too narrow to share.

question.text: Which habits keep bicyclists safe?

answer.text: Bicyclists should wear a helmet, never slip between a truck or bus and the curb, and ride on the right with the flow of traffic.

teaching.text: Asked "Which habit keeps bicyclists safe?" a tempting wrong answer is "Riding against traffic", but ride with traffic. Remember: Helmet, right side, no squeezing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists should wear a helmet, never slip between a truck or bus and the curb, and ride on the right with the flow of traffic.

question.text: What lights must a bicycle have at night?

answer.text: Tennessee law requires a bicycle ridden at night to have a front lamp showing white light visible for at least five hundred feet and a red reflector or red lamp visible from five hundred feet behind.

teaching.text: Asked "How far must a bicycle's front white lamp be visible at night?" a tempting wrong answer is "Fifty feet", but at least five hundred feet. Remember: White front, red rear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tennessee law requires a bicycle ridden at night to have a front lamp showing white light visible for at least five hundred feet and a red reflector or red lamp visible from five hundred feet behind.

question.text: What should you expect from children on bicycles?

answer.text: Children on bicycles cannot judge traffic well, so expect erratic moves and sudden turns wherever children may be riding.

teaching.text: Asked "Children are riding bicycles nearby. What should you expect?" a tempting wrong answer is "Perfect signals", but expect erratic moves. Remember: Expect sudden moves.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children on bicycles cannot judge traffic well, so expect erratic moves and sudden turns wherever children may be riding.

question.text: Where can bicycles appear suddenly?

answer.text: Watch for bicycles coming out of driveways or from behind parked cars and other obstructions.

teaching.text: Asked "Where should you watch for bicycles appearing suddenly?" a tempting wrong answer is "Only at bike shops", but from driveways and behind parked cars. Remember: Driveways and parked cars.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Watch for bicycles coming out of driveways or from behind parked cars and other obstructions.

question.text: What does a pennant flag on a bicycle often mean?

answer.text: A red or orange pennant flag on a bicycle commonly means the rider has impaired hearing, so slow down.

teaching.text: Asked "A bicycle has a red or orange pennant flag. What does it commonly mean?" a tempting wrong answer is "The rider is racing", but impaired hearing. Remember: Flag means hearing loss.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A red or orange pennant flag on a bicycle commonly means the rider has impaired hearing, so slow down.

question.text: Why are motorcycles hard to see and judge?

answer.text: A motorcycle's narrow, short profile makes it harder to see and makes its distance and speed harder to judge.

teaching.text: Asked "Why is a motorcycle's speed and distance hard to judge?" a tempting wrong answer is "Its loud engine", but its narrow, short profile. Remember: Narrow means hidden.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A motorcycle's narrow, short profile makes it harder to see and makes its distance and speed harder to judge.

question.text: What causes most car-motorcycle crashes?

answer.text: Research shows two-thirds of car-motorcycle crashes are caused by the car driver turning in front of the motorcycle, often without ever seeing it.

teaching.text: Asked "According to research, what causes two-thirds of car-motorcycle crashes?" a tempting wrong answer is "Motorcycles speeding", but car drivers turning in front. Remember: Cars turn in front.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Research shows two-thirds of car-motorcycle crashes are caused by the car driver turning in front of the motorcycle, often without ever seeing it.

question.text: May you share a lane with a motorcycle?

answer.text: Motorcycles are entitled to the full width of a lane, so never try to share a lane with one.

teaching.text: The full lane for motorcycles rule gives a motorcycle the full lane, while the passing a motorcycle rule says to pass it like a car but not too close or fast. Remember: Full lane for motorcycles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles are entitled to the full width of a lane, so never try to share a lane with one.

question.text: How should you pass a motorcycle?

answer.text: Pass a motorcycle as you would a car, but not too close or too fast, because the blast of air can push the rider out of control.

teaching.text: The full lane for motorcycles rule gives a motorcycle the full lane, while the passing a motorcycle rule says to pass it like a car but not too close or fast. Remember: Not too close, not fast.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass a motorcycle as you would a car, but not too close or too fast, because the blast of air can push the rider out of control.

question.text: How far should you follow a motorcycle?

answer.text: Allow at least a two-second following distance behind a motorcycle so the rider has time to maneuver or stop.

teaching.text: Asked "What following distance should you allow behind a motorcycle?" a tempting wrong answer is "Half a second", but at least two seconds. Remember: Two seconds behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Allow at least a two-second following distance behind a motorcycle so the rider has time to maneuver or stop.

question.text: Why check blind spots for motorcycles before changing lanes?

answer.text: Motorcyclists riding alongside a lane of cars are often out of view, so check your blind spots before changing lanes.

teaching.text: Asked "Before changing lanes, why check your blind spots for motorcycles?" a tempting wrong answer is "Motorcycles always honk", but they are often out of view. Remember: Riders hide alongside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcyclists riding alongside a lane of cars are often out of view, so check your blind spots before changing lanes.

question.text: What should you wait for at intersections with a motorcycle?

answer.text: At intersections, where most motorcycle crashes happen, wait until the rider's intention to turn or go straight is clear before pulling into the rider's path.

teaching.text: Asked "At an intersection, a motorcycle approaches. When should you pull into its path?" a tempting wrong answer is "Right away", but wait until intent is clear. Remember: Wait for clear intent.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At intersections, where most motorcycle crashes happen, wait until the rider's intention to turn or go straight is clear before pulling into the rider's path.

question.text: Why are motorcycles hard to judge at night?

answer.text: At night a motorcycle's single headlight or taillight can blend with other lights and make its distance hard to judge, so dim your high beams for it as for any vehicle.

teaching.text: Asked "At night, a motorcycle approaches with one headlight. What should you do with your high beams?" a tempting wrong answer is "Keep them on", but dim them. Remember: One light blends in.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At night a motorcycle's single headlight or taillight can blend with other lights and make its distance hard to judge, so dim your high beams for it as for any vehicle.

question.text: Which road conditions trouble motorcyclists most?

answer.text: Wet roads, crosswinds, truck wind blasts, railroad crossings and metal grated bridges all cause extra trouble for motorcyclists, so give them more room.

teaching.text: Asked "Which road condition causes extra trouble for motorcyclists?" a tempting wrong answer is "Smooth dry pavement", but metal grated bridges. Remember: Give riders more room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Wet roads, crosswinds, truck wind blasts, railroad crossings and metal grated bridges all cause extra trouble for motorcyclists, so give them more room.

question.text: Which vehicles accelerate fastest and slowest?

answer.text: Motorcycles accelerate faster than any other vehicle, while trucks and buses are the slowest.

teaching.text: Asked "Which vehicles accelerate the fastest?" a tempting wrong answer is "Trucks", but motorcycles. Remember: Motorcycles fast, trucks slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles accelerate faster than any other vehicle, while trucks and buses are the slowest.

question.text: Who suffers most deaths in car-truck crashes?

answer.text: In crashes between cars and large trucks, the people in the car, usually the driver, suffer seventy-eight percent of the deaths.

teaching.text: Asked "In crashes between cars and large trucks, who suffers most of the deaths?" a tempting wrong answer is "The truck driver", but the people in the car. Remember: Car people die most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In crashes between cars and large trucks, the people in the car, usually the driver, suffer seventy-eight percent of the deaths.

question.text: What is the most important protection in a truck crash?

answer.text: A safety belt is the single most important protection in a crash with a large truck.

teaching.text: Asked "What is the single most important protection in a crash with a large truck?" a tempting wrong answer is "A big car", but a safety belt. Remember: Belt up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A safety belt is the single most important protection in a crash with a large truck.

question.text: When can't the truck driver see you?

answer.text: If you cannot see the truck driver in the truck's mirror, the truck driver cannot see you.

teaching.text: The see the trucker's mirror rule says if you cannot see the trucker in the mirror the trucker cannot see you, while the truck no-zones rule maps the no-zones in front, beside and behind. Remember: No mirror face, no view.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you cannot see the truck driver in the truck's mirror, the truck driver cannot see you.

question.text: How do truck weight and stopping compare with a car?

answer.text: A loaded tractor-trailer may weigh up to eighty thousand pounds, and a car at fifty-five miles per hour can stop in about two hundred forty feet while a truck at that speed needs about four hundred fifty feet or more.

teaching.text: Asked "At fifty-five miles per hour, about how far does a truck need to stop?" a tempting wrong answer is "About two hundred forty feet", but that is for a car. Remember: Trucks need far more.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A loaded tractor-trailer may weigh up to eighty thousand pounds, and a car at fifty-five miles per hour can stop in about two hundred forty feet while a truck at that speed needs about four hundred fifty feet or more.

question.text: How much do communities depend on trucks?

answer.text: Trucks are the only delivery and pickup method for about seventy-seven percent of America's communities, and a tractor-trailer combination can be longer than seventy feet.

teaching.text: Asked "For about what share of America's communities are trucks the only delivery method?" a tempting wrong answer is "About seven percent", but about seventy-seven percent. Remember: Trucks deliver most.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks are the only delivery and pickup method for about seventy-seven percent of America's communities, and a tractor-trailer combination can be longer than seventy feet.

question.text: How do trucks make right turns?

answer.text: Trucks must swing wide to the left to make a right turn, and they cannot see cars or motorcycles directly behind or beside them.

teaching.text: Asked "A truck ahead signals a right turn and swings left. What is happening?" a tempting wrong answer is "The driver changed plans", but trucks swing wide to turn right. Remember: Trucks swing wide left.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks must swing wide to the left to make a right turn, and they cannot see cars or motorcycles directly behind or beside them.

question.text: What can cutting in front of a truck force?

answer.text: Cutting in front of a truck or bus can force an emergency stop it cannot make in time, so look for its front in your mirror before pulling in.

teaching.text: Asked "What can cutting in front of a truck force?" a tempting wrong answer is "A friendly honk", but an emergency stop it cannot make. Remember: Never cut off trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Cutting in front of a truck or bus can force an emergency stop it cannot make in time, so look for its front in your mirror before pulling in.

question.text: When can you move back in front of a truck you passed?

answer.text: After passing a truck, do not move back in front of it until you can see the whole front of the truck in your rearview mirror, and do not slow down once you are ahead.

teaching.text: The return after passing a truck rule says to wait until the whole front of the truck shows in your mirror, while the headlight blink signal rule says a blink of its headlights signals you may move back. Remember: Whole front in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After passing a truck, do not move back in front of it until you can see the whole front of the truck in your rearview mirror, and do not slow down once you are ahead.

question.text: Where are a truck's blind spots?

answer.text: A truck's blind spots cover the area right in front of it, along both sides and up to two hundred feet behind it.

teaching.text: The see the trucker's mirror rule says if you cannot see the trucker in the mirror the trucker cannot see you, while the truck no-zones rule maps the no-zones in front, beside and behind. Remember: Front, sides, far behind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A truck's blind spots cover the area right in front of it, along both sides and up to two hundred feet behind it.

question.text: How much can a long-hood trucker miss in front?

answer.text: A trucker with a long hood may not see the first ten to twenty feet in front of the bumper.

teaching.text: The truck no-zones rule lists the no-zones, and the long hood blind area rule adds that a long hood can hide the first ten to twenty feet in front. Remember: Ten to twenty feet hidden.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A trucker with a long hood may not see the first ten to twenty feet in front of the bumper.

question.text: How should you exit near a truck?

answer.text: Do not drive directly behind a truck or bus, and if you are exiting, slow down and exit behind the truck instead of cutting in front of it.

teaching.text: Asked "You need to exit and a truck is beside you. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Cut in front", but exit behind it. Remember: Exit behind trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not drive directly behind a truck or bus, and if you are exiting, slow down and exit behind the truck instead of cutting in front of it.

question.text: Why do trucks often seem slower than they are?

answer.text: Because of their size, trucks and buses often look slower than they really are.

teaching.text: Asked "Why do trucks and buses often look slower than they really are?" a tempting wrong answer is "Because of their color", but because of their size. Remember: Size fools the eye.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Because of their size, trucks and buses often look slower than they really are.

question.text: What does a trucker's headlight blink after you pass mean?

answer.text: If a truck or bus driver blinks the headlights after you pass, it signals that you may move back in, once you can see the truck's front in your mirror.

teaching.text: The return after passing a truck rule says to wait until the whole front of the truck shows in your mirror, while the headlight blink signal rule says a blink of its headlights signals you may move back. Remember: Blink means come back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a truck or bus driver blinks the headlights after you pass, it signals that you may move back in, once you can see the truck's front in your mirror.

question.text: Which lane should you avoid near a weigh station?

answer.text: Avoid the right lane near a commercial vehicle weigh station so slow trucks can merge back onto the road.

teaching.text: Asked "Near a commercial vehicle weigh station, which lane should you avoid?" a tempting wrong answer is "The left lane", but the right lane. Remember: Leave the right lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Avoid the right lane near a commercial vehicle weigh station so slow trucks can merge back onto the road.

question.text: Where should you wait behind a truck on an uphill grade?

answer.text: On an uphill grade, keep to the left side of your lane while waiting behind a truck so its driver can see you, and leave extra room in case it rolls back.

teaching.text: The behind a truck uphill rule says to keep left and leave room behind a truck uphill, while the trucks downhill rule says trucks go faster downhill so keep your speed after passing one. Remember: Keep left, leave room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On an uphill grade, keep to the left side of your lane while waiting behind a truck so its driver can see you, and leave extra room in case it rolls back.

question.text: What should you do while a truck passes you?

answer.text: When a truck passes you, keep to the far side of your lane and slow slightly, and never speed up while a truck or bus is passing.

teaching.text: The when a truck passes you rule tells you to keep to the far side and slow slightly as a truck passes you, while the meeting a truck rule tells you to keep right when meeting one. Remember: Far side, slow slightly.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When a truck passes you, keep to the far side of your lane and slow slightly, and never speed up while a truck or bus is passing.

question.text: How should you position yourself when meeting a truck?

answer.text: When meeting a truck from the opposite direction, keep as far right as you can, because the wind turbulence between vehicles pushes them apart.

teaching.text: The when a truck passes you rule tells you to keep to the far side and slow slightly as a truck passes you, while the meeting a truck rule tells you to keep right when meeting one. Remember: Keep right when meeting.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When meeting a truck from the opposite direction, keep as far right as you can, because the wind turbulence between vehicles pushes them apart.

question.text: What should you do after passing a truck downhill?

answer.text: Trucks lose speed climbing hills but travel faster downhill, so after passing one on a downgrade keep your speed instead of slowing in front of it.

teaching.text: The behind a truck uphill rule says to keep left and leave room behind a truck uphill, while the trucks downhill rule says trucks go faster downhill so keep your speed after passing one. Remember: Keep speed after passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks lose speed climbing hills but travel faster downhill, so after passing one on a downgrade keep your speed instead of slowing in front of it.

question.text: What should you do about truck spray in rain?

answer.text: In rain or standing water, a truck's spray can badly cut your vision, so move as far from it as you can within your lane.

teaching.text: Asked "In rain, a truck's spray badly cuts your vision. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Move closer", but move away within your lane. Remember: Move away from spray.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In rain or standing water, a truck's spray can badly cut your vision, so move as far from it as you can within your lane.

question.text: Why never cross behind a truck about to back up?

answer.text: Never cross behind a truck that is getting ready to back up, since you will be in the driver's blind spots.

teaching.text: Asked "A truck is preparing to back up. Why should you never cross behind it?" a tempting wrong answer is "It is always safe", but you will be in its blind spots. Remember: Backing trucks cannot see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never cross behind a truck that is getting ready to back up, since you will be in the driver's blind spots.

question.text: What does a truck with smoking wheels downhill mean?

answer.text: If a truck going downhill has smoking wheels or is moving too fast, it may have lost its brakes, so fall back and do not pass.

teaching.text: Asked "A truck going downhill has smoking wheels. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Pass it quickly", but do not pass. Remember: Lost brakes, fall back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a truck going downhill has smoking wheels or is moving too fast, it may have lost its brakes, so fall back and do not pass.

question.text: Why not follow hazardous materials trucks closely?

answer.text: Do not follow too closely behind trucks carrying hazardous materials, which make frequent stops such as at railroad crossings.

teaching.text: Asked "Why not follow hazardous materials trucks too closely?" a tempting wrong answer is "They are slow only uphill", but they stop often. Remember: Hazmat trucks stop often.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not follow too closely behind trucks carrying hazardous materials, which make frequent stops such as at railroad crossings.

question.text: May you stop in a runaway truck ramp?

answer.text: Never stop or park in a runaway truck ramp, which exists to stop out-of-control trucks and buses on steep downgrades.

teaching.text: Asked "May you stop or park in a runaway truck ramp?" a tempting wrong answer is "Yes, briefly", but never. Remember: Ramps are for runaways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never stop or park in a runaway truck ramp, which exists to stop out-of-control trucks and buses on steep downgrades.

question.text: Who are most children killed in school bus crashes?

answer.text: Most children killed in school bus crashes are pedestrians aged five to seven, hit by the bus or by drivers illegally passing a stopped school bus.

teaching.text: The school bus deaths rule says most children killed are pedestrians hit near the bus, and the ten-foot danger zone rule says children stay ten feet away, so stop far enough back. Remember: Young pedestrians near buses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most children killed in school bus crashes are pedestrians aged five to seven, hit by the bus or by drivers illegally passing a stopped school bus.

question.text: When do most school bus pedestrian deaths happen?

answer.text: Nearly three of every four school bus pedestrian deaths happen while children are getting on or off the bus.

teaching.text: Asked "When do nearly three of every four school bus pedestrian deaths happen?" a tempting wrong answer is "While the bus is moving fast", but while getting on or off. Remember: Boarding and leaving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Nearly three of every four school bus pedestrian deaths happen while children are getting on or off the bus.

question.text: How far do children stay from a school bus?

answer.text: Children are taught to stay ten feet from a school bus and take five giant steps away from it, so drivers must stop far enough back to leave that space.

teaching.text: The school bus deaths rule says most children killed are pedestrians hit near the bus, and the ten-foot danger zone rule says children stay ten feet away, so stop far enough back. Remember: Ten feet away.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Children are taught to stay ten feet from a school bus and take five giant steps away from it, so drivers must stop far enough back to leave that space.

question.text: Which vehicles show the slow-moving vehicle emblem?

answer.text: Animal-drawn vehicles, most farm vehicles and construction equipment must display the slow-moving vehicle emblem, a fluorescent or reflective orange triangle, on the rear.

teaching.text: Asked "What is the slow-moving vehicle emblem?" a tempting wrong answer is "A red circle", but an orange triangle. Remember: Orange triangle means slow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Animal-drawn vehicles, most farm vehicles and construction equipment must display the slow-moving vehicle emblem, a fluorescent or reflective orange triangle, on the rear.

question.text: How does farm machinery behave on the road?

answer.text: Farm machinery usually has no turn signals, may swing wide left before turning right, and usually travels under twenty-five miles per hour

teaching.text: Asked "A farm tractor ahead swings left. What might it be about to do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Pass you", but it may be about to turn right. Remember: Slow and wide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Farm machinery usually has no turn signals, may swing wide left before turning right, and usually travels under twenty-five miles per hour

question.text: What rights do animal-drawn vehicles have?

answer.text: Animal-drawn vehicles have the same rights to the road as motor vehicles and must follow the same rules.

teaching.text: Asked "What rights do animal-drawn vehicles have on the road?" a tempting wrong answer is "None", but the same rights. Remember: Same rights, same rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Animal-drawn vehicles have the same rights to the road as motor vehicles and must follow the same rules.

question.text: What should you check before passing a slow-moving vehicle?

answer.text: Slow-moving vehicles may turn into unmarked entrances, so make sure the driver has seen you and knows you intend to pass before you go around.

teaching.text: Asked "Before passing a slow-moving vehicle, what should you make sure of?" a tempting wrong answer is "That you are speeding", but the driver has seen you. Remember: Be sure they see you.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Slow-moving vehicles may turn into unmarked entrances, so make sure the driver has seen you and knows you intend to pass before you go around.

question.text: How should you pass a horse on the road?

answer.text: When approaching or passing a horse being ridden or led along the road, use due care, keep a reasonable speed and distance, and do not honk or rev your engine.

teaching.text: Asked "You are approaching a horse being ridden along the road. What should you do?" a tempting wrong answer is "Honk so the rider knows you are there", but do not honk. Remember: Quiet and careful.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When approaching or passing a horse being ridden or led along the road, use due care, keep a reasonable speed and distance, and do not honk or rev your engine.

question.text: What does orange mean on a road sign?

answer.text: Work zone signs have an orange background with black letters or symbols, and the color orange always means road work ahead, slow down.

teaching.text: The orange work zone signs rule says orange signs mean road work ahead, while the work zone speeding fine rule sets a fine of up to five hundred dollars for speeding where workers are present. Remember: Orange means road work.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Work zone signs have an orange background with black letters or symbols, and the color orange always means road work ahead, slow down.

question.text: What is the fine for speeding where work zone workers are present?

answer.text: In Tennessee, speeding in a reduced-speed work zone where transportation or construction workers are present brings a fine of up to five hundred dollars.

teaching.text: The orange work zone signs rule says orange signs mean road work ahead, while the work zone speeding fine rule sets a fine of up to five hundred dollars for speeding where workers are present. Remember: Up to five hundred.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In Tennessee, speeding in a reduced-speed work zone where transportation or construction workers are present brings a fine of up to five hundred dollars.

question.text: How much time does a work zone sign give at sixty miles per hour?

answer.text: A car going sixty miles per hour covers eighty-eight feet per second, so a Road Work one thousand five hundred Feet sign leaves you only seventeen seconds before the work zone.

teaching.text: The seventeen seconds rule shows how little time a sign gives at sixty miles per hour, while the headlights in work zones rule says to turn on headlights and stay in your lane in the zone. Remember: Seventeen seconds.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A car going sixty miles per hour covers eighty-eight feet per second, so a Road Work one thousand five hundred Feet sign leaves you only seventeen seconds before the work zone.

question.text: When should you merge for a closing lane in a work zone?

answer.text: Merge as soon as you learn a lane is closing ahead in a work zone; a last-chance merger can be ticketed and blamed for a crash.

teaching.text: Asked "You learn a lane is closing ahead in a work zone. When should you merge?" a tempting wrong answer is "At the last possible moment", but merge as soon as you learn. Remember: Merge early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Merge as soon as you learn a lane is closing ahead in a work zone; a last-chance merger can be ticketed and blamed for a crash.

question.text: What should you do before and in a work zone?

answer.text: Turn on your headlights before entering a work zone, and do not change lanes inside it unless told to.

teaching.text: The seventeen seconds rule shows how little time a sign gives at sixty miles per hour, while the headlights in work zones rule says to turn on headlights and stay in your lane in the zone. Remember: Lights on, stay put.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn on your headlights before entering a work zone, and do not change lanes inside it unless told to.

question.text: What kind of crash is most common in work zones?

answer.text: Most work zone crashes are rear-end collisions, so do not tailgate and keep a safe distance from barriers, equipment and workers.

teaching.text: Asked "What kind of crash is most common in work zones?" a tempting wrong answer is "Head-on crashes", but rear-end collisions. Remember: Rear-end crashes lead.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most work zone crashes are rear-end collisions, so do not tailgate and keep a safe distance from barriers, equipment and workers.

question.text: What do mobile work zones mean for drivers?

answer.text: Mobile work zones such as line painting, patching and mowing mean workers may be ahead even if not yet visible, so heed the signs until you pass the End Road Work sign.

teaching.text: Asked "In a mobile work zone, how long should you heed the work signs?" a tempting wrong answer is "Until you see a worker", but until the End Road Work sign. Remember: Heed signs to the end.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Mobile work zones such as line painting, patching and mowing mean workers may be ahead even if not yet visible, so heed the signs until you pass the End Road Work sign.

question.text: Why must drivers always yield to trains?

answer.text: Drivers must always yield the right-of-way to trains, because a train cannot stop quickly; one going fifty-five miles per hour needs a full mile to stop.

teaching.text: The always yield to trains rule says to always yield to trains, which need a mile to stop, while the fifty to fifteen feet rule sets the stopping distance from the rail. Remember: Trains need a mile.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Drivers must always yield the right-of-way to trains, because a train cannot stop quickly; one going fifty-five miles per hour needs a full mile to stop.

question.text: How much deadlier is a train crash than a car crash?

answer.text: Your chance of dying in a crash with a train is about thirty times higher than in a crash with a car or even a large truck.

teaching.text: Asked "How does your chance of dying in a train crash compare with a car crash?" a tempting wrong answer is "About the same", but about thirty times higher. Remember: Trains are thirtyfold deadlier.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your chance of dying in a crash with a train is about thirty times higher than in a crash with a car or even a large truck.

question.text: Where do most train-car collisions happen?

answer.text: Over half of train-car collisions happen at crossings with lights, bells or gates, and most occur within twenty-five miles of the driver's home.

teaching.text: Asked "Where do most train-car collisions occur?" a tempting wrong answer is "Far from home", but within twenty-five miles of home. Remember: Near home, signaled crossings.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Over half of train-car collisions happen at crossings with lights, bells or gates, and most occur within twenty-five miles of the driver's home.

question.text: How far from the rail must you stop at a signaled crossing?

answer.text: At a railroad crossing with electric or mechanical signals, a driver who must stop has to do so within fifty feet but no closer than fifteen feet from the nearest rail.

teaching.text: The fifty to fifteen feet rule sets where to stop at a crossing with signals, while the stop sign crossings rule requires a complete stop at a crossing with a stop sign. Remember: Fifty to fifteen feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a railroad crossing with electric or mechanical signals, a driver who must stop has to do so within fifty feet but no closer than fifteen feet from the nearest rail.

question.text: What must you do at a crossing with a stop sign?

answer.text: At a railroad crossing with a stop sign, come to a complete stop and cross only after looking both ways for a train.

teaching.text: The fifty to fifteen feet rule sets where to stop at a crossing with signals, while the stop sign crossings rule requires a complete stop at a crossing with a stop sign. Remember: Full stop, look both ways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a railroad crossing with a stop sign, come to a complete stop and cross only after looking both ways for a train.

question.text: May you drive around lowered crossing gates?

answer.text: Never drive around lowered crossing gates; stay stopped until the gates are fully up and the lights have stopped flashing.

teaching.text: The never go around gates rule says to wait until gates are up and lights stop, while the second train rule says to check for a second train on multiple tracks. Remember: Never go around.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive around lowered crossing gates; stay stopped until the gates are fully up and the lights have stopped flashing.

question.text: What if the lights start while you are on the tracks?

answer.text: If the lights start flashing or the gates begin to lower while you are already on the tracks, keep moving across and never back up.

teaching.text: The keep moving across rule says to keep moving if the lights start while you are on the tracks, while the stalled on the tracks rule says to get out if your vehicle stalls there. Remember: Keep moving across.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If the lights start flashing or the gates begin to lower while you are already on the tracks, keep moving across and never back up.

question.text: What must you check after a train passes on multiple tracks?

answer.text: Where there is more than one track, make sure a second train is not coming from either direction before you cross after a train passes.

teaching.text: The never go around gates rule says to wait until gates are up and lights stop, while the second train rule says to check for a second train on multiple tracks. Remember: Watch for a second train.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Where there is more than one track, make sure a second train is not coming from either direction before you cross after a train passes.

question.text: What if your vehicle stalls on the tracks?

answer.text: If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, everyone should get out at once and move away from the tracks, even if no train is in sight, then call the number on the blue Emergency Notification System sign or nine hundred eleven.

teaching.text: The keep moving across rule says to keep moving if the lights start while you are on the tracks, while the stalled on the tracks rule says to get out if your vehicle stalls there. Remember: Get out, call.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle stalls on the tracks, everyone should get out at once and move away from the tracks, even if no train is in sight, then call the number on the blue Emergency Notification System sign or nine hundred eleven.

question.text: Which way should you run from a stalled car as a train comes?

answer.text: If a train is coming toward your stalled vehicle, run toward the train at a forty-five-degree angle away from the tracks to avoid flying debris.

teaching.text: Asked "A train is coming toward your stalled vehicle. Which way should you run?" a tempting wrong answer is "Straight down the tracks", but away at an angle toward the train. Remember: Toward the train, angled.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If a train is coming toward your stalled vehicle, run toward the train at a forty-five-degree angle away from the tracks to avoid flying debris.

question.text: Which vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing?

answer.text: School buses, passenger buses and trucks carrying hazardous materials must stop at every railroad crossing, and you must never pass them there on a two-way road.

teaching.text: The vehicles that must stop rule lists the vehicles that must stop at every crossing, while the passing at multi-lane crossings rule says when you may pass them on a multi-lane road. Remember: Buses and hazmat stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: School buses, passenger buses and trucks carrying hazardous materials must stop at every railroad crossing, and you must never pass them there on a two-way road.

question.text: When may you pass a bus stopped at a multi-lane crossing?

answer.text: On a multi-lane road, do not pass a bus or hazardous materials truck stopped at a crossing unless the crossing's signals or gates are clearly not activated.

teaching.text: The vehicles that must stop rule lists the vehicles that must stop at every crossing, while the passing at multi-lane crossings rule says when you may pass them on a multi-lane road. Remember: Only if signals are off.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a multi-lane road, do not pass a bus or hazardous materials truck stopped at a crossing unless the crossing's signals or gates are clearly not activated.

question.text: Who must wear a belt in a fifteen-passenger van?

answer.text: Tennessee law requires every occupant of a fifteen-passenger van to wear a safety belt at all times.

teaching.text: Asked "Who must wear a safety belt in a fifteen-passenger van in Tennessee?" a tempting wrong answer is "Only the driver", but every occupant. Remember: Every van rider belts.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tennessee law requires every occupant of a fifteen-passenger van to wear a safety belt at all times.

question.text: Do you need a special license to drive a fifteen-passenger van?

answer.text: No special endorsement or license is needed to drive a fifteen-passenger van in Tennessee, but the driver should be trained and experienced.

teaching.text: Asked "Do you need a special endorsement to drive a fifteen-passenger van in Tennessee?" a tempting wrong answer is "Yes, a commercial license", but no endorsement is needed. Remember: No endorsement, need skill.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: No special endorsement or license is needed to drive a fifteen-passenger van in Tennessee, but the driver should be trained and experienced.

question.text: How should you load a fifteen-passenger van?

answer.text: In a fifteen-passenger van, seat passengers as far forward as possible and do not tow trailers or load the roof, which raise rollover risk.

teaching.text: Asked "How should passengers be seated in a fifteen-passenger van?" a tempting wrong answer is "All in the back", but as far forward as possible. Remember: Seat forward, no roof load.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a fifteen-passenger van, seat passengers as far forward as possible and do not tow trailers or load the roof, which raise rollover risk.

question.text: How do recreational vehicles handle?

answer.text: Recreational vehicles handle more like large trucks, need longer stopping distances and have many blind spots.

teaching.text: Asked "How do recreational vehicles handle?" a tempting wrong answer is "Like sports cars", but more like large trucks. Remember: RVs drive like trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Recreational vehicles handle more like large trucks, need longer stopping distances and have many blind spots.
